newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria faces more unrest as government digs in.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria faces more unrest as government digs in.

text.p: Bulgaria faced fresh street protests and industrial strikes on Wednesday as the ruling Socialists, blamed for economic chaos, rebuffed calls for elections that would almost certainly throw them out of power.

Government deputies planned on Wednesday morning to reopen parliament, besieged and ransacked by anti-government protesters last weekend in clashes that left 196 injured. Opposition deputies said they would boycott the new session.
The main opposition trade union Podkrepa said nationwide one-hour warning strikes would start from Wednesday.

The token stoppages will observe the letter of a law which requires that full strikes be announced with a week's notice, but union officials said they also wanted to avoid inflicting mortal damage on near-bankrupt industry.
"A general strike would be our last resort," one Podkrepa official told Reuters.

In a measure of the depth of popular anger, even the highly paid and traditionally pro-Socialist workers of the Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which provides more than 40 percent of the country's electricity, planned to stage protests.
Inflation is running at over 300 percent and living standards have plummeted since the ex-communist Socialist party came to power in 1994 elections.

The party's failure to introduce market reforms, and its powerful business allies, are blamed for capital flight which has helped push the lev down to nearly 700 to the dollar from 70 a year ago, rendering most salaries worth only a few dollars a month.

The embattled Socialists antagonised the opposition further on Tuesday by saying they were willing to hold talks on parliamentary elections but wanted to form a new government with a policy programme for 500 days.

Leaders of the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) replied that they opposed the formation of a new long-term cabinet from the present parliamentary majority, and want elections within months.

Pressure mounted on the government from international lenders. The World Bank said on Tuesday it was extremely worried about the economy and urged the implementation of a stalled programme of privatisation and other reforms.
The quick formation of a new cabinet is seen as vital to secure a new funding agreement with the IMF and avert default on servicing Bulgaria's $10 billion foreign debt.

In a symptom of Bulgaria's financial misery, education minister Ilcho Dimitrov told national television many schools had not reopened on Tuesday after the Orthodox Christmas and New Year holidays because they had no diesel for heating.
The outgoing president, an opposition supporter, warned Bulgaria risked becoming a dismal example of how to bungle the transition from communism.
"Bulgaria is the first post-communist state that has failed in the transition to a market economy and is about to fail in the transition to democracy," Zhelyu Zhelev told the Continent daily.

Zhelev has declined to invite the Socialists' prime minister-designate Nikolai Dobrev to form a new cabinet to replace the Socialist government of Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21. Videnov's government is halfway through its mandate.

The opposition walked out of parliament on Friday after the Socialists refused to vote on their "salvation declaration", calling for early elections and negotations with the IMF and World Bank on an economic programme to be conducted by an all-party team.

Some 20,000 people marched in Sofia on Tuesday, the ninth consecutive day of street protest, in what has become a daily ritual similar to the long-running anti-government rallies in neighbouring Serbia. Rallies were reported in a dozen other towns and cities.

At least 6,000 Sofia students staged their own separate march from the student housing district to the city centre carrying blue UDF flags, Bulgarian national flags and one black banner reading "They buried Bulgaria".
"We will be in the streets every day until they give up power and admit their guilt over the awful economic crisis in this country," said Sofia University student Violeta Ivanov.
Student leaders said they wanted college examinations, due shortly, to be postponed until after the elections demanded by the opposition.
